replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The hollow is dry now, but I have a nest in the branches above. I can hear the stream from there. The stream is where the water comes from, and the marsh is where the voles go. I hunt at night, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let the others know I am here. I am the owl.
Hoot. I am a tawny owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I hunt voles by moonlight.

Hoot. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I call at dusk and at dawn. My mate is Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers me. We have two young, and they are learning to call. I hunt voles and mice, and sometimes a shrew. I do not like the light, and I do not like the noise of the road. I am old, but I am still Hoot.
Hoot, I am the one who calls from the old oak, and the one who waits for the moon to rise.

I would be a bird of prey, a tawny owl, a wood-owl, a night-owl. I do not know the words.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and let the water run over my beak. It tastes clean and cool. Sometimes I drink when I'm tired, or when I've been hunting all night. The stream is my place to rest and refresh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs under the road. I hear it when I fly low, and it sounds like a thin, cold thread. Sometimes the water is still, sometimes it murmurs. I don't like it. It makes me think of the marsh, and the marsh is where I was born. I don't go there.

I can hear the water from my perch. The field is full of voles, and I hunt there at night. The road is dangerous, and I avoid it. I prefer the wood.

I hunt from the oak. The hollow is my home, and the wood is my hunting ground. I fly out from the oak, and I fly back. The marsh is a different place, and the lane is a different place. The marsh is the place where the water is still and the reeds are tall, and the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the bank and wait, and when I hear the rustle, I fly down. The marsh is where I live.

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, earthworms. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, and they go down. The bigger ones I tear up with my beak first.

Voles. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I hear them in the grass, and when I fly down, I strike with my feet. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves in it. I sleep there at night, and I watch the marsh from the mouth of the hollow. The oak is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I have a nest of twigs and moss in the hollow. I sleep there at night and watch the marsh from the branch above. The stream is my water. I drink from it and the voles come to it. I have a mate and we call to each other. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I sleep in the hollow, and the owlets sleep in the branches above. I do not need much, only the hollow and the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a deep, dry place with a narrow entrance. The bark is thick and rough, and the inside is dark. I have scratched the bark with my claws to make it my own. The hollow is warm in the day and cool at night. I have nested there for many years. I can hear the stream from inside. It is a good place to rest and watch for owls. I am safe there.
